sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV

steps.title: Install pandas and load CSV
steps.instructions: Install pandas (pip install pandas or uv add pandas), put orders.csv next to main.py, and read it with pd.read_csv. Print the DataFrame and run it with uv run main.py.
hints: Which pandas function reads a comma-separated file?
Use pd.read_csv with the file name and store the result in df.
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"); print(df). Then run uv run main.py from the folder that holds the CSV.
common_mistakes: Running the script from a different folder, which raises FileNotFoundError for orders.csv
Installing pandas globally but running inside a uv environment that does not have it
Using pip instead of pip3 on Mac or Linux

steps.title: Load data in Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create a new Jupyter notebook (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P, then 'New Jupyter Notebook'), save it as notebook.ipynb, and load orders.csv in the first cell. Print df in a second cell and run each cell separately.
hints: Notebook cells keep variables in memory between runs.
Install the Python extension, then create a .ipynb file and pick a Python kernel.
Put the import and read_csv in cell 1 and print(df) in cell 2, then run both.
common_mistakes: Choosing a kernel that does not have pandas installed
Running the print cell before the load cell, which gives NameError: df

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: Inspect the data with df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index, each in its own cell. Check the row count and the column types.
hints: Which methods show the first and last rows?
info() lists the column dtypes; describe() summarizes the numeric columns.
Run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index in separate cells.
common_mistakes: Writing df.columns() with parentheses, which fails because columns is an attribute
Forgetting the parentheses on head/info, which shows the bound method instead of the data

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: Select one column with df['Country'] (a Series) and several with df[['Country','Product']] (a DataFrame). Get rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10], and read a field such as df.iloc[10]['Country'].

explanations.topic: A list of columns returns a DataFrame

hints: Columns are selected with square brackets and the column name.
Pass a list inside the brackets to get several columns back.
df[['Country','Product']] for columns; df.iloc[10] for the 11th row.
common_mistakes: Using single brackets with two names, df['Country','Product'], which raises KeyError
Calling iloc with parentheses instead of brackets
Mistyping column-name capitalization

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions
steps.instructions: Filter with boolean masks such as df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'], combined with & and | with each condition in parentheses. Also try comparisons on Quantity, .str.startswith/.str.endswith, .isin([...]) and ~ to negate.
hints: A comparison on a column returns True/False for every row.
Put that comparison inside df[...] to keep only the True rows.
Wrap each condition in parentheses and join them with & or |, e.g. df[(cond1) & (cond2)].
common_mistakes: Filtering on the wrong column (Product instead of Category) and getting an empty table
Using Python 'and'/'or' instead of &/|
Leaving out parentheses around each condition
Forgetting that str.endswith is case-sensitive

steps.title: Update values with loc
steps.instructions: Use df.loc[mask, 'Column'] = value to change matching rows, e.g. set Product to 'Tim' for Anna and Country from 'USA' to 'United States'. Then uppercase the whole column with df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().

explanations.topic: Row mask plus column in loc

hints: loc takes two things: which rows and which column.
The rows can be a boolean mask like df['Country'] == 'USA'.
df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
common_mistakes: Chained assignment like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ..., which triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and does not update df
Mistyping the column name, which silently creates a new column
Calling str.upper without parentheses

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with df = df.drop(39) and confirm with df.tail(). Clean with df.dropna(), fillna with inplace=True, and rename a column with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True).

explanations.topic: drop removes a row by index

hints: drop returns a new DataFrame unless you assign it back.
dropna removes missing values and fillna replaces them.
df.rename(columns={'old': 'new'}, inplace=True) renames a column.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning it back, so df is unchanged
Running drop(39) twice, which raises KeyError because the label is already gone
Forgetting inplace=True and expecting rename to change df

steps.title: Analyze with groupby and sorting
steps.instructions: Count rows per country with df['Country'].value_counts() and total the price per country with df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum(). Sort with df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False).
hints: Which method counts how often each value appears?
groupby takes the column to group by; then pick the column to aggregate.
df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()
common_mistakes: Forgetting to select the Price column before .sum(), which sums every column
Writing ascending='False' as a string instead of the boolean False
Expecting USA in the results after uppercasing countries without reloading the data

steps.title: Save DataFrame to CSV
steps.instructions: Write the modified DataFrame to a new file with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False). Confirm that new_file.csv appears in the explorer.
hints: The method mirrors read_csv.
Use df.to_csv with a file name.
df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
common_mistakes: Leaving the index on, which adds an extra unnamed column when the file is reloaded
Overwriting orders.csv by accident
